fixes.explanation: I get why that seems possible, friend, but the text says otherwise. After Saul's warning, “…the Kenites moved away from the Amalekites.” They were told to go on and get away, and they went. I think that's a smart move when somebody warns you.

That's right, the Kenites listen. Verse 6 ends with “So the Kenites moved away from the Amalekites.” Saul warned them, and they moved away. Me, I've ignored a warning or two in my day, mostly about the oven.

Eglon was king of Moab (Judges 3:12), which is another nation altogether. The Amalekite king Saul captures alive is Agag. I mix up names all the time too. Ask me which of my cookie cutter kids is Berry and which is Buttercup and I'd get it right, but ask me on a bad day and who knows.
Best, friend. Saul and his troops spared “…the best of the sheep and cattle, the fat calves and lambs, and the best of everything else.” Verse 9 puts it plainly. Best is the word to remember.
Weakest isn't the word here, baker. The text says they spared “…the best of the sheep and cattle…” That's the opposite of weakest. The best is what they kept.

That's the one. The text says “…they devoted to destruction all that was despised and worthless.” In this verse, the best is what they were unwilling to devote. So Saul and his troops spared the best and devoted what was despised and worthless.

Not here, baker. The LORD says, “I regret that I have made Saul king…” That's the word, regret. He goes on to say Saul “…has turned away from following Me and has not carried out My instructions.” The LORD gives His reason right there in the verse.

There's no rejoicing in this verse, friend. The LORD says, “I regret that I have made Saul king, for he has turned away from following Me and has not carried out My instructions.” Regret is the word He uses. I think it's a heavy thing to read.
Samuel was distressed, and he “…cried out to the LORD all that night.” The text puts his night with the LORD. I think that tells you how much it hit him.

The text doesn't mention Samuel calling the elders, friend. It says Samuel “…was distressed and cried out to the LORD all that night.” That's what the verse gives for his night. I think he was hurting.

No letter is mentioned in this scene, friend. Samuel's night is this: “…Samuel was distressed and cried out to the LORD all that night.” Then, “Early in the morning Samuel got up to confront Saul…” (1 Samuel 15:12).
Saul never says that, baker. He says the best were spared “…to sacrifice to the LORD your God…” Feeding the troops isn't in his answer. That's the reason he gives.

That's it. Samuel says, “Behold, obedience is better than sacrifice, and attentiveness is better than the fat of rams.” Saul kept pointing at sacrifices, and Samuel points at listening. Obeying the LORD's voice is what he says is better.

No sickness in this verse, baker. Samuel says, “Because you have rejected the word of the LORD, He has rejected you as king.” Saul has rejected the word of the LORD, and Samuel says the LORD has rejected him as king. His words are about Saul's place as king, not about his health.
Samuel says no, baker. His words are, “I will not return with you…” He adds that Saul has rejected the word of the LORD, and the LORD has rejected him as king over Israel. That's a firm no.

The kingdom, baker. Samuel says, “The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today…” Right before this, Saul grabbed the hem of Samuel's robe, and it tore (1 Samuel 15:27). A robe tears, and then Samuel speaks of a kingdom torn.

The blessing on his family isn't what Samuel names, baker. He says, “The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today and has given it to your neighbor who is better than you.” What's torn away is the kingdom, and it's given to his neighbor.
Samuel doesn't say son, baker. He says the LORD “…has given it to your neighbor who is better than you.” That's the word he uses. He doesn't give a name in this verse.

Crown isn't what Saul asks for. He says, “Please honor me now before the elders of my people and before Israel.” The word is honor, friend. He wants it in front of the elders of his people and before Israel.

Defend isn't in the request, baker. Saul says, “Please honor me now before the elders of my people and before Israel.” Back in verse 25 he asked Samuel to forgive his sin. Now the ask is for honor, and he wants it before the elders and before Israel.
Gibeah, baker. The text says Samuel went to Ramah, “…but Saul went up to his home in Gibeah of Saul.” They go separate ways after this. Gibeah is the home the text names for Saul.
The text says no, baker. “And to the day of his death, Samuel never again visited Saul.” That's how long it held. This line is heavy.

False, friend. The text says, “And to the day of his death, Samuel never again visited Saul. Samuel mourned for Saul…” So Samuel did not visit him again. I think that's a sad ending to this part of the story.
